lessons.title: Mediation and dispute resolution
lessons.description: Learn language for mediation and alternative dispute resolution.

vocabulary.example: The parties agreed to try mediation.
The mediator met with both parties.
The mediator helps facilitate discussion.
Each party reviewed the proposal.
They hope to resolve the dispute.

sections.heading: Professional dialogue
sections.body:
A: Would your client consider mediation?
B: We are open to discussing the proposal.
A: The mediator can help the parties explore options.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: Use neutral phrases such as “explore options” and “seek a resolution” to avoid implying that a party has already accepted an offer.

quiz.question: Who facilitates mediation?
quiz.explanation: A mediator facilitates discussion between parties.

quiz.question: What does resolve a dispute mean?
options: Find a way to settle it
quiz.explanation: To resolve a dispute is to settle or solve it.

lessons.title: Legal research and citations
lessons.description: Read and discuss legal sources, authorities and citations in English.

vocabulary.example: The judgment cites a relevant authority.
The provision sets out the filing period.
The statute governs the procedure.
Please verify the citation.
The lawyer discussed a relevant precedent.

sections.heading: Research note
sections.body: The memorandum identifies the statutory provision, explains its wording and cites the authority relied upon.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: Distinguish the source from the argument: “The statute provides…” reports a text; “This suggests…” introduces an interpretation.

quiz.question: What is a statutory provision?
options: A section or rule in legislation
quiz.explanation: A provision is a part of a law that sets out a rule.

quiz.question: What should you do with a legal citation?
quiz.explanation: Legal citations should be checked against the actual source.

lessons.title: Written submissions and legal arguments
lessons.description: Structure a concise written submission with issues, reasons and requested relief.
objectives: Connect facts to a legal argument

vocabulary.example: Counsel filed written submissions.
The appeal raises one ground.
The argument relies on the wording of the statute.
Accordingly, the applicant requests relief.
The prayer for relief appears at the end.

sections.heading: Model paragraph
sections.body: For the reasons set out above, the applicant submits that the decision should be reconsidered. Accordingly, the applicant respectfully requests the relief stated below.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: A clear submission identifies the issue, gives reasons supported by sources, then states the requested order. Local court rules determine required form and terminology.

quiz.question: What is a ground of appeal?
options: A reason relied on to challenge a decision
quiz.explanation: A ground states a reason why a decision is challenged.

quiz.question: Which phrase introduces a conclusion?
quiz.explanation: Accordingly signals a conclusion or result.

lessons.title: Client communication and legal costs
lessons.description: Explain fees, disbursements and next steps to a client in clear language.

vocabulary.example: The lawyer explained the fee.
The filing fee is a disbursement.
This is an estimate of the likely costs.
The office sent an invoice.
The engagement letter defines the scope of work.

sections.heading: Client email example
sections.body: Dear Client, our current estimate covers the work described in the engagement letter. Court fees and other disbursements may be charged separately. We will contact you before any material change to the scope of work.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: Avoid promising a fixed total unless the engagement terms support it. Explain assumptions, exclusions and the next update in plain language.

quiz.question: A disbursement is usually…
options: An expense paid on behalf of the client
quiz.explanation: A disbursement is an expense paid for a client, such as a filing fee.

quiz.question: What defines the scope of work?
options: The work agreed with the client
quiz.explanation: The scope of work describes the legal services covered by the engagement.

lessons.title: Greeting a client at reception
lessons.description: Use simple greetings and identity questions in a legal office.

vocabulary.example: The client is here.
The lawyer is in the office.
What is your name?
I have an appointment.
Please wait here.

sections.heading: Dialogue
sections.body: Receptionist: Good morning. What is your name?\nVisitor: My name is Ali. I have an appointment.\nReceptionist: Thank you. Please wait here.

sections.heading: Language focus
sections.body: Use “What is your name?” to ask for a name and “I have an appointment” to explain why you are visiting. In a real office, follow local confidentiality and visitor procedures.

quiz.question: Which sentence tells reception you have a meeting arranged?
quiz.explanation: An appointment is an arranged meeting.

quiz.question: Who may receive legal advice from a lawyer?
quiz.explanation: A client is the person receiving professional legal services.

quiz.question: Choose a polite instruction.
quiz.explanation: Please makes the instruction more polite.

lessons.title: Arranging a client appointment
lessons.description: Ask about dates, times and basic documents for an appointment.
objectives: Ask when a client is available

vocabulary.example: Are you available on Tuesday?
Please confirm the appointment.
Please bring the document.
The appointment is at noon.
Can we reschedule the meeting?

sections.heading: Dialogue
sections.body:
Lawyer: Are you available on Tuesday at noon?
Client: Yes, I am.
Lawyer: Please bring the contract and your identification document.
Client: I will bring them.

sections.heading: Language focus
sections.body: Use “Are you available…?” to ask about availability. Use “Could you bring…?” for a polite request. Confirm the date and time clearly to avoid misunderstandings.

quiz.question: Which phrase asks politely for a document?
options: Could you bring the contract, please?
Bring it because I said so.
quiz.explanation: Could you… please? is a polite request.

quiz.question: What does reschedule mean?
quiz.explanation: To reschedule is to change the planned date or time.

quiz.question: Which detail should be confirmed for an appointment?
quiz.explanation: Confirming date and time prevents scheduling confusion.

lessons.title: Narrating facts in a client interview
lessons.description: Use past simple and sequence markers to report a client's account clearly.

vocabulary.example: The incident occurred on Monday.
According to the client, the payment was made.
The parties subsequently exchanged letters.
The claimant alleges that the goods were damaged.
Please record the date of the call.

sections.heading: Interview note
sections.body: According to the client, the agreement was signed in March. The goods arrived two weeks later, but several items were missing. The client subsequently sent a written complaint. The supplier has not yet responded.

sections.heading: Language focus
sections.body: Use the past simple for completed events. Sequence markers such as first, later and subsequently help establish chronology. “Allege” attributes a claim to a party; it does not mean the allegation has been proven.

quiz.question: Which verb introduces a claim that is not yet established as fact?
quiz.explanation: Allege reports a party's assertion without treating it as proven.

quiz.question: Which phrase helps show chronology?
quiz.explanation: Subsequently means later or after that.

quiz.question: Why write “according to the client”?
options: To identify the source of the account
quiz.explanation: Attribution distinguishes a person's account from an independently established fact.

lessons.title: Structuring written legal submissions
lessons.description: Organize a legal submission around issues, authority, analysis and relief.

vocabulary.example: The central issue is whether notice was valid.
The submission relies on statutory authority.
The interpretation depends on the wording of the provision.
Accordingly, the appellant requests that the order be set aside.
The relief sought is stated in the final section.

sections.heading: Model structure
sections.body: Issue: whether the notice complied with the contract. Rule: the relevant clause requires written notice. Analysis: the email record indicates that notice was sent before the deadline, although receipt remains disputed. Conclusion: the court is respectfully asked to determine whether the contractual requirement was satisfied.

sections.heading: Legal-language caution
sections.body: A persuasive submission separates the issue, governing rule, application to facts and conclusion. The terms “appellant”, “claimant”, “applicant” and “petitioner” vary by procedural posture and jurisdiction; use the term adopted by the relevant court.

quiz.question: What does “relief sought” identify?
quiz.explanation: Relief sought states what the party asks the court to order.

quiz.question: A strong legal submission should…
options: Connect authority to the facts and requested result
quiz.explanation: Legal analysis explains how the relevant rule applies to the facts.

quiz.question: Why should procedural party labels be checked by jurisdiction?
options: Their meanings and use can differ between systems
They are identical in every court
They never appear in legal writing
quiz.explanation: Procedural terminology depends on the court and legal system.

lessons.title: Comparing legal terminology across systems
lessons.description: Explain why similar English legal terms may have different meanings across jurisdictions.

vocabulary.example: The court's jurisdiction depends on the statute.
There is no exact equivalence between the two terms.
Precedent has a different role across legal systems.
The rule is codified in a statute.
The translation is context-dependent.

sections.heading: Comparative note
sections.body: The English word “equity” can refer to a body of doctrine in some common-law systems, while in ordinary financial writing it may mean ownership value. A translation should therefore identify the field, jurisdiction and procedural context before selecting an Arabic equivalent.

sections.heading: Translation method
sections.body: Avoid one-to-one substitution when institutions differ. State the source jurisdiction, explain the function of the institution, and use a short explanatory gloss if the target system has no direct equivalent.

quiz.question: What should guide translation of a jurisdiction-specific term?
quiz.explanation: Legal translation requires functional and contextual analysis.

quiz.question: If no exact equivalent exists, the translator should…
options: Explain the concept and qualify the translation
quiz.explanation: An explanatory gloss can preserve meaning without claiming false equivalence.

quiz.question: Why is “equity” potentially ambiguous?
options: It has different legal and ordinary meanings
It always means the same thing
It is never used in law
quiz.explanation: The term's meaning changes with legal system and context.

lessons.title: Drafting a qualified legal opinion
lessons.description: Draft nuanced legal analysis that distinguishes settled rules, factual uncertainty and risk.

vocabulary.example: On the present record, the claim appears arguable.
The conclusion is subject to verification of the original document.
The discrepancy may be material to liability.
The outcome is contingent upon the court's findings.
In the alternative, the client may seek compensation.

sections.heading: Opinion extract
sections.body: On the present record, the claim appears arguable, subject to verification of the signed original and the applicable limitation period. The discrepancy may be material if the court finds that it affected performance. The likely outcome remains contingent upon the evidence admitted and the court's interpretation of the governing provision.

sections.heading: Drafting discipline
sections.body: Distinguish a legal rule from a factual assumption and a prediction. “May”, “likely” and “subject to” should reflect the actual degree of uncertainty. Procedural phrases such as “in the alternative” must match the remedies available under the relevant law.

quiz.question: What does “on the present record” signal?
options: The assessment is based on currently available materials
The case has already been decided
quiz.explanation: The phrase limits the opinion to the evidence currently available.

quiz.question: A conclusion “subject to verification” is…
options: Conditional on checking a relevant fact or document
A statement that no evidence matters
quiz.explanation: The conclusion depends on a verification step.

quiz.question: Why use “may” in a legal opinion?
options: To reflect a qualified possibility where appropriate
quiz.explanation: Modal verbs should express the level of certainty supported by the analysis.
